topic: the difference between a solvent's polarity and solubility (like dissolves like)

easy.text: The rule 'like dissolves like' suggests that polar solvents (like water) tend to dissolve what kind of solutes best?

options.feedback: Correct -- polar solvents generally dissolve other polar or ionic substances well.
Nonpolar substances generally dissolve poorly in polar solvents like water -- that's the opposite of this rule.
Solid metal dissolution isn't what this general solubility rule is describing.

options.text: Nothing at all -- polar solvents dissolve nothing
options.feedback: Polar solvents like water are actually excellent at dissolving many substances, particularly other polar or ionic ones.

medium.text: Oil (nonpolar) doesn't mix well with water (polar). What does this demonstrate about the 'like dissolves like' principle?

options.text: Substances with different polarities (one polar, one nonpolar) tend to not mix or dissolve well together
options.feedback: Correct -- this mismatch in polarity is exactly why oil and water famously separate rather than mix.

options.text: Oil and water should actually mix perfectly according to this rule
options.feedback: This is backwards -- the rule specifically predicts that mismatched polarities (like oil and water) WON'T mix well.

options.text: This principle doesn't apply to liquids at all
options.feedback: This principle applies broadly to solubility, including liquid-liquid mixing scenarios like oil and water.

options.text: Oil has no polarity classification at all
options.feedback: Oil is specifically classified as nonpolar -- that classification is exactly what explains its poor mixing with polar water.

hard.text: Soap can help mix oil and water together because soap molecules have both a polar (hydrophilic) end and a nonpolar (hydrophobic) end. How does this dual structure allow soap to bridge the two substances?

options.text: The nonpolar end of soap molecules surrounds oil droplets while the polar end interacts with water, effectively linking the two otherwise incompatible substances together
options.feedback: Correct -- this dual-affinity structure is exactly what allows soap to act as an emulsifier, letting oil and water mix in a stable way.

options.text: Soap actually removes all polarity from both oil and water
options.feedback: Soap doesn't eliminate polarity from either substance -- its own dual-ended structure is what bridges the two, not by altering their inherent properties.

options.text: Soap molecules are entirely nonpolar, just like oil
options.feedback: Soap molecules specifically have BOTH a polar and a nonpolar end -- that dual nature is exactly what gives it its bridging ability.

options.text: This has nothing to do with polarity at all
options.feedback: This effect is entirely explained by soap's dual-polarity molecular structure, directly relevant to the like-dissolves-like principle.

easy.hard: Substances sharing a similar charge-distribution pattern tend to interact and blend most effectively.
easy.medium: Substances with a similar type of charge distribution tend to mix well together.
easy.easy: Similar types of substances tend to mix well together.

medium.hard: Consider whether these two substances share the same or different type of charge distribution across their molecules.
medium.medium: Water is polar and oil is nonpolar -- think about whether "like dissolves like" predicts they'd mix or not.
medium.easy: Since oil and water are different types (nonpolar vs polar), think about whether they'd mix well.

hard.hard: Soap's amphiphilic structure (having both hydrophilic and hydrophobic regions) lets one end associate with each of the two otherwise-incompatible substances, forming a stable connecting bridge.
hard.medium: One end of the soap molecule likes to stick to oil, and the other end likes to stick to water, connecting the two together.
hard.easy: One end of the soap molecule sticks to oil, and the other end sticks to water, connecting the two.
